extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy / economic history
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length exposition on causes of agricultural stagnation, the rise and progress of towns and cities after the fall of the Roman Empire, and how commerce and manufactures influenced country improvement. Intended as a historical/political-economy account rather than prescriptive policy guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppressive public taxes (tallage/tailles) discourage improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The taille (tax upon supposed profits estimated by the stock on the farm) and similar tallages/tenths/fifteenths compelled tenants to appear to have as little stock as possible, discouraging employment and improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: French 'taille'—farmers hide or refrain from accumulating stock because the tax makes employing stock on the land uneconomic; the taille is 'almost equal to a prohibition' of employing accumulated stock. Comparable ancient English taxes (tenths and fifteenths) had similar effects where they affected land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenancy reduces incentive to improve land compared to proprietorship
rubrics_metrics.description: A farmer (tenant) improves land more slowly than a proprietor because a large share of produce is consumed by the rent, analogous to trading with borrowed money versus one's own capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: with equal conduct the proprietor's stock can improve faster because profits are not eaten by rent; the farmer lacks the same ability to reinvest produce into land improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social status and honor deter capital entering farming
rubrics_metrics.description: Because farmers and yeomanry were socially regarded as inferior to merchants and master manufacturers, men of considerable stock seldom leave superior social stations to become farmers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: little transfer of stock from other professions into farming, limiting capital available for agricultural improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of exportation of corn hinders cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient policies that universally prohibited exportation of corn (without special licence) discouraged cultivation, as seen in ancient Italy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: prohibition of exportation plus encouragement of importation obstructed cultivation of fertile Italy; such restraints reduce incentives for less-fertile countries to cultivate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraints on inland commerce (anti-engrosser/regrater/forestaller laws) impede agricultural improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurd laws against engrossers, regraters, forestallers, and privileges of fairs and markets restricted inland commerce of farm produce and thereby discouraged cultivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These restraints limited the internal trade in produce and reduced market opportunities for growers, decreasing incentives to increase production or improve land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market access (ready local market) encourages cultivation and improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial and manufacturing towns afford a great and ready market for rude produce, encouraging cultivation and further improvement, particularly for neighbouring countryside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The nearer market reduces carriage costs so traders can pay growers better prices while keeping consumer prices competitive, increasing returns to cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban legal privileges (freedom of burghers) enable economic independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Grants that allowed inhabitants to give away daughters in marriage, have their children succeed to goods, and dispose of effects by will removed attributes of villanage and created true freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such privileges converted formerly servile town inhabitants into free burghers, facilitating accumulation, credit access, and enterprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granting town revenues 'in fee' with perpetual rent fosters municipal autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Letting the farm of the town in fee (for ever) with a rent certain converted personal exemptions into perpetual, corporate privileges and established free burghs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change made exemptions communal (belonging to the burgh) and often accompanied creation of corporations with magistrates, bye-laws, and municipal jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal self-government (magistrates, bye-laws, militia) creates security and order
rubrics_metrics.description: Erecting towns into commonalties/corporations with magistrates, councils, bye-laws, walls, and obligations like watch and ward established order and enabled collective defence and internal jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects: internal disputes (except crown pleas) decided locally; exemption from other courts; capacity to compel inhabitants to pay farm-rent; greater security and independence from barons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual defence leagues and urban militias protect towns and enable independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Inhabitants entering into leagues of mutual defence and organizing militias made towns capable of resisting lords and, in some regions, becoming independent republics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Italian and Swiss cities where sovereign authority waned—cities conquered local nobility, forced them to pull down castles, and often became republics (e.g., Berne, many Italian republics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign support of towns as counterweights to barons
rubrics_metrics.description: Sovereigns granted privileges and farms to towns to secure their support against great lords; towns thereby became allies of the crown and a counterbalance in assemblies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: kings who were weakest with their barons were often most liberal in grants (e.g., King John of England). Town deputies later represented burghs in states-general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cities draw capital and labour from the countryside because of legal sanctuary and security
rubrics_metrics.description: If an industrious cultivator could conceal himself in a town for a year, he became free; thus towns acted as sanctuaries where accumulated stock could be secure and attract country capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: accumulated stock in hands of rural workers tended to be transferred to towns, enabling urban industry and manufacturing growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic access to sea or navigable rivers expands city's market and permits grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities near the sea-coast or navigable rivers can draw materials and subsistence from far beyond their neighbourhood, exchanging manufactured goods or acting as carriers between distant countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such cities can grow opulence even while surrounding countryside is poor; examples include Venice, Genoa, Pisa during the crusades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two origins of manufactures for distant sale: merchant-established vs organic refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufactures for distant sale emerge either (1) by merchants/undertakers imitating foreign manufactures using foreign materials, or (2) naturally by refinement of household/coarser local manufactures based on domestic materials and agricultural surplus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: merchant-driven—silk in Lucca moved to Venice, Lyons silk using foreign silk, Spitalfields; organic—Leeds, Halifax, Sheffield cloths grew from local refinement and agriculture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufactures introduced by merchants often rely on foreign raw materials and privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: When manufacturers are established by projects of individuals, they frequently use foreign materials and are sometimes located in maritime cities; privileges and incentives (e.g., offers by emigrant families) aided establishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Venetian silk initially used Sicilian and Levant materials; Lucca silk families introduced to Venice with privileges; Spitalfields unlikely to source materials from England.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agricultural surplus in inland fertile regions fosters local manufactures
rubrics_metrics.description: Inland, fertile countries produce surplus provisions that make provisions cheap and attract workmen who refine local materials into manufactures, saving carriage costs and creating value locally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: refined manufactures are higher value/low bulk and can be exported to distant markets, effectively exporting the value of the agricultural surplus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merchants buying and investing in land are often superior improvers to country gentlemen
rubrics_metrics.description: Merchants who become country gentlemen tend to invest capital in profitable improvements, whereas mere country gentlemen typically spend rather than invest, making merchants better improvers of land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: mercantile habits of order, economy, and attention predispose merchants to undertake large capital improvements when profitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce and manufactures introduce order, good government, liberty, and security that stimulate non-subsistence industry
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond markets and capital, perhaps the most important effect of commerce/manufactures is introducing order and security, enabling individuals to aim at conveniences and elegancies beyond mere subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast: in pre-commercial societies, surplus produce maintained retainers and hospitality; with commerce, surplus is exchanged, reducing private retinues and promoting productive industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refined manufactures can 'virtually export' agricultural produce
rubrics_metrics.description: Refined, compact manufactures can embody the value of large quantities of rude produce (e.g., fine cloth contains the price of many thousand weight of corn) and thus be exported more easily than raw agricultural goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: countries unable to export raw produce due to carriage costs can still access distant markets through manufactured goods that concentrate value in small bulk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban militia can be more readily assembled and give cities a military advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: City militias could be assembled quicker than rural forces, which often gave towns the advantage in disputes with neighbouring lords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contributed to towns' capacity to resist baronial aggression and to secure autonomy or favorable concessions.
